task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 31, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Marshfield Harbor Container Terminal completed its automation transition in 2021; of 220 workers employed before automation, 50 now work at the terminal in supervisory and maintenance roles.

Former crane operator Maria Chen, 48, was among the 170 workers who did not retain a job at the automated terminal; she accepted a retraining package in 2022 and completed a 14-month logistics technology program.
Chen said: "I was offered retraining. I took it. I graduated. The job I retrained for pays twenty-two percent less than the job I lost. Nobody mentioned that part in the brochure."
David Nkrumah, 44, is one of 50 workers who accepted a supervisor position at the automated terminal; he oversees 12 autonomous guided vehicles on the day shift.
Nkrumah said: "I stayed because I knew the terminal. I know where the problems happen before the sensors flag them. The machine has data. I have context. They still need both."
The terminal operator, company Marshfield Pacific Logistics, said automation increased throughput by 34% and reduced cargo handling errors by 61%; labor costs fell by 58%.

Union representative Frank Santos, who represented Marshfield workers during the transition, said the productivity gains accrued to the terminal operator and its shipping customers; the displaced workers received an average severance of $28,000 and retraining vouchers worth up to $18,000.
Santos said: "The deal kept the terminal competitive. That's true. But the people who made it competitive for thirty years were the ones who paid for the change. That's also true."
Chen completed her retraining and works in supply chain software support; she earns $62,000 per year compared to her pre-automation wage of $79,000.

Nkrumah earns $91,000 per year, up from $82,000 as a crane operator; he said the additional pay reflects the additional responsibility and shift compression — he now manages more equipment with fewer colleagues.

A labor economist at Northview University, Dr. Anika Solis, said the Marshfield transition follows a documented pattern: automation at the productivity frontier creates a small number of higher-wage jobs and a larger number of displaced workers who do not fully recover income.

Dr. Solis said: "We call it net positive because total employment in logistics is not falling. We are less careful about whether the specific workers displaced are the ones who get the new jobs. Often they are not."

Marshfield Pacific Logistics said it contributed $4.2 million to a regional workforce development fund as part of the automation transition agreement with the union; the fund supported 240 retraining completions.
Santos said 240 completions covers fewer than half of the 170 displaced workers; he did not have data on how many of the completers found employment in their new field.

Chen said she is not angry at the company: "Automation was coming. Anyone who watched the industry knew that. What I'm angry about is the gap between what the transition package promised and what it actually delivered."

Nkrumah said he worries about the next wave: predictive maintenance software is advancing rapidly, and some of the diagnostic work he does may itself be automated: "I supervise the machines that replaced my colleagues. I'm watching to see if the machines will supervise me."

Dr. Solis said the policy response has not kept pace: retraining programs are designed for workers who will find equivalent employment; they are less effective for workers who will find lower-paying employment and need income support during the gap.

Santos said the union's next negotiation will include provisions for income continuation, not just retraining; he said that battle is harder because the terminal is now profitable and has less financial pressure to negotiate.
Chen said she tells younger workers in the industry: "Get certified in something that doesn't run on rails. The rails are going automatic."
Nkrumah said what he misses most is not the crane but the teamwork: "Twelve guys on a shift, everyone knowing their job. Now it's me and a screen. It's efficient. It's also lonely."
